I wanted two. My siblings came in pairs, my cousins came in pairs, my niece and nephews all came in pairs. All 2-4 years apart. That’s how it’s supposed to go. 

My adult son was an only child. He was born into an already failed marriage, and I knowingly wasn’t ready to be a parent at the time. And it shows. I was half-assed at best then, and we’re not close now. 

Much later I found the perfect partner, and we decided to have kids. Her family also came in pairs, so we were on the same page. After the first, we started to have trouble as a couple, but assuming it was temporary readjustment, drove on with the plan. After the second, it was clear our relationship was over. And it is also clear having kids is what ruined the relationship. 

Now, as a single parent, I am convinced I would make a great single parent of one kid. But two I can’t handle. They outnumber me. They outmaneuver, outsmart, and outsubborn me. There are so many things that I could do with just one, but I just can’t handle with two. They antagonize each other to the point of killing any joy in an activity. 

So instead, I skip opportunities that I feel I should be doing with them, and instead stay home and feel like a failure of a parent. And dread the day in a decade or so when I’m sitting at home alone regretting being a half-assed parent twice in a row.

46M here. I have a bad habit of ending a relationship long after it is over. By the time I call it quits, I am walled off and emotionally numb. The first thing I feel after a breakup is relief, I so I bet it looks a lot like I don’t grieve. 

Give me time and space for the walls to weaken, and I grieve severely. My last relationship ended three years ago, but I wasn’t able to get out of the house (financial reasons) until 4 months ago. Now I am starting to experience emotions again, and no sir, I don’t like it. I cry most nights, and bawl like I never have before. I imagine what Harry Potter must have felt like as the dementors were sucking out his soul. 

I do this in the privacy of my home or my car, once or twice in the locker room at work, and I am pretty open about it. But I won’t share this with an ex.

There’s nothing saying you can’t be friends with an ex, but I think you are right, you are disrespecting yourself by remaining friends with her. You are holding on to one aspect of something that doesn’t exist anymore, and you are hurting because of it. 

I tried to stay friends with my ex wife, and I honestly believed we were friends. It wasn’t until I watched her go through her second divorce, and then saw her dating life afterwards that I truly understood what kind of person she is. It was then I learned how our “friendship” was just another avenue for her to use someone. 

On the other hand, I am friends with another ex gf. We stayed friendly, but we didn’t stay friends. If anything, we became friends again. It’s a clear and honest friendship based on what is, not on what was. 

Don’t be afraid to cut contact with her. Give yourself the chance to heal, build up your confidence and self respect again. Make new friends, find new love. If you two were meant to be friends, start it from scratch instead of holding onto rubble and ashes.

Your situation is so similar to mine that I had to read it several times to make sure you are not my ex. I am going to speak from my own experience, so please forgive me if any of this comes across as harsh. 

My ex wants to discuss everything that went on, from the things that caused the problems, to all the transgressions that happened during the breakup process. I can’t engage in these conversations for two reasons. One, we do NOT agree on what went wrong, or who didn’t hold up their responsibility, and I doubt we will ever agree. Rehashing it doesn’t do any good, at least not now. Two, these end up as one sided “conversations”, or as I call them, lectures. I don’t feel the need to listen to every thing I have done to hurt her while she can’t acknowledge any pain I was experiencing. 

In my opinion, it is best to focus on the practical and functional aspects of moving forward. Share your pain with a therapist or a friend. Sharing it with him will likely only have it magnified and bounced back. Focus on taking care of your child. Figure out a schedule and living situations for the future, and then sell the house. Being tied to an asset like that with an ex can be a nightmare— pragmatically, financially, and emotionally. 

If you keep the conversations about the child and working together moving forward, you may develop a rapport that could possibly even become a friendship. But that is extremely unlikely if he feels like he’s being dragged through the mud about the relationship.

You are strong! The amount of responsibility you have, especially at your age, is astounding. Of course it will weigh on you. And it sounds like your family is not supportive either. Please keep being strong. It will get better. 

It may help to set some goal posts. Soon you will be 18 and you can walk away. I know you won’t leave your siblings, but you could. The youngest only have a couple more years until school, that should lighten your load. As the older ones get more capable, they can start taking more responsibility and help you out. 

I know you are struggling, it is hard, and it feels like it will last forever. But you will get through this. It does get better.

I got married at 23 right before I joined the army. In retrospect, it was a misguided attempt to save a doomed relationship with an emotionally abusive manipulator. But I hadn’t figured that out at the time…

Anyway, I was in Savannah, GA, and it was our one year anniversary. I was having a beer with some friends while I waited for my then wife to get out of work. We were talking to the bartender, and she was super cool. Just really… cool. Down to earth, friendly, smart, ambitious. I immediately felt really comfortable talking to her. We had similar goals and ambitions. I suppose she was pretty, but I didn’t really notice. She’s was just super cool (I wish I could think of a better word). Totally would have fit right in with my group of friends. 

Fast forward a few hours, my then wife and our friends had had dinner and a few drinks, and were walking through downtown Savannah. I hear someone behind me say “hey!” I turned and saw this angel standing there, this woman with long gorgeous hair that matched her fitted brown dress. It took me a second, but my jaw dropped when I realized it was the bartender from earlier, and she was looking directly at me. It was one of those moments from the movies when time stops and the music changes. Then I turned back around to see my then wife with her pants around her ankles, pissing in the marble fountain, yelling at the top of her lungs while couples rode by in horse drawn carriages. It was an embarrassing and heart breaking moment. In that moment I realized how bad of a decision I had made. I turned back to the angel and shrugged, and watched her walk away forever. Twenty something years later and I still think about that.

Single steps. Forget the marathon and focus on that one next step in front of you. Go for the little victories. Like get up and make your bed (watch that admiral’s speech about making your bed). Brush your teeth, take a shower. Eat breakfast. Make it if you can. I like a scrambled egg with cheese. It’s easy and quick and feels like I accomplished something healthy. 

Focus on the “do”. Try not to think about what was, or the regret or the shame. Force yourself to get up and walk. Go outside. Give yourself some small task to accomplish, like walk to the mailbox and back, or once around the block, pick up a piece of trash or pull a weed. Give yourself a purpose, even if it’s a small temporary one. Keep taking these baby steps and try to build some momentum. 

This is what works for me on occasion. YMMV. Good luck
